overview: The file contains two brief State Department records concerning Japanese news and propaganda activity abroad in 1938. A cross-reference sheet points to a Military Attaché report on Japanese newspaperman Kinjiro Watanabe’s efforts in Mexico City to deny allegations of Japanese espionage circulating in the Central American press. An internal Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizes the opening of a Domei News Agency office in Hong Kong, noting its failure to attract Chinese newspaper subscribers, its limited clientele, and suspicions that its purpose was to disseminate Japanese propaganda.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Military Attaché report on Kinjiro Watanabe
subfiles.about: The sheet refers researchers to a report on Japanese newspaperman Kinjiro Watanabe’s response to allegations of Japanese espionage in the Central American press.
subfiles.summary: This filing sheet cross-references report no. 4280, dated April 26, 1938, under the separate personal file for Kinjiro Watanabe. It describes Watanabe as a Japanese newspaperman living in Mexico City who denied and belittled espionage charges reprinted by the Central American press from an article in KEN.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Domei News Agency office in Hong Kong
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes a Hong Kong telegram concerning the establishment, clientele, and suspected propaganda purpose of Domei’s new local office.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum summarizes Hong Kong telegram no. 176 of May 10, 1938, reporting that Domei opened a regular Hong Kong office on May 1 under Robert Y. Horiguchi. Consul General Southard believed that the office had been created solely to distribute Japanese propaganda. Although Domei solicited more than twenty Chinese newspapers, none subscribed; its reported clients were the Hong Kong Telegraph, the Hong Kong Press, and a Japanese afternoon daily. The memorandum also records a rumor that the Hong Kong Press received subsidies from the German and Japanese governments.

interest: The file offers a compact view of how U.S. officials tracked Japanese information activity across widely separated overseas press environments shortly before the Second World War. It is especially useful for connecting individual journalists, official news agencies, espionage narratives, and alleged newspaper subsidies to broader concerns about Japanese propaganda. The contrast between Watanabe’s rebuttal of espionage accusations in Latin America and Domei’s unsuccessful solicitation of Chinese newspapers in Hong Kong also shows that Japanese influence efforts were neither uniform nor necessarily successful.
